Related-party service contracts 15–40% of RP fees 0.5–1.5pp IRR Iraq, Kazakhstan, Malaysia
Non-routine capital (platform modifications, major workovers) 20–50% challenged 0.3–1.0pp IRR Nigeria, Russia (pre-2022)
Pre-development exploration costs 0–100% (jurisdictional) 0.5–2.0pp IRR Indonesia, Bangladesh
Abandonment provisions (pre-MWP approval) 100% until approved by NOC Timing-dependent Nigeria, Angola

4-step IC adjustment workflow:

  1. Flag audit-risk jurisdictions: In the Country Profile, check the Reform History tab for “Tax dispute” or “Cost audit” event types and a Stability Score ≤ 2. Frequent fiscal disputes correlate with aggressive cost audit posture. Nigeria, Indonesia, Iraq-KRG, Kazakhstan, and Bangladesh are established high-risk jurisdictions.
  2. Quantify exposure by cost category: Estimate related-party service fees and allocated G&A as a % of gross opex. Apply the challenge rates from the table above to size the disallowance exposure in dollars and as an equivalent opex uplift factor.
  3. Run Scenario Builder with audit-risk adjustment: Increase Opex/bbl by the audit-risk factor — typically ×1.12–1.25 for high-risk PSC jurisdictions (Nigeria, Indonesia, Iraq), ×1.05–1.10 for medium-risk (Angola, Malaysia, Egypt), ×1.02–1.05 for low-risk (Norway, UK, Australia). This simulation shows the IRR impact of partial or full disallowance of the at-risk cost pool.
  4. IC memo disclosure: “Cost recovery audit risk estimated at [X]% of G&A allocation and related-party services, equivalent to [Y]pp IRR impact ($[Z]M NPV reduction). Adjustment applied in Scenario Builder (opex +[W]%); ORCA statutory take of [T]% assumes full cost recovery to ceiling and does not reflect audit-risk disallowances.”

Rule of thumb by jurisdiction tier:

  • High audit risk (Nigeria, Indonesia, Iraq-KRG, Kazakhstan, Bangladesh): Build 5–8% opex uplift for disallowance exposure. Flag in IC memo. Consider AIPN JOA audit dispute clause and whether local cost audit is subject to international arbitration.
  • Medium audit risk (Angola, Malaysia, Egypt, Libya): 3–5% opex uplift; note in model assumptions. Review PSC cost recovery definitions article for specific exclusions.
  • Low audit risk (Norway, UK, Australia, UAE): Standard opex; no adjustment typically warranted. HMRC, Petroleum Safety Authority, and ATO audits are rules-based and arm’s-length; challenge rates on properly structured intercompany agreements are low.

Interaction with cost recovery cap: Disallowances reduce realized cost recovery below the stated ceiling. In a deepwater PSC with a 50% cost recovery cap and $200M/year gross opex, a 20% disallowance on G&A reduces realized recovery by approximately $8–12M/year — equivalent to 0.5–1.0pp IRR reduction on a $1.2B reference project. The effect is largest when the project is operating near the cost recovery ceiling and smallest when cost oil is already well below the cap (excess cost oil accumulated).

Source: ORCA v219 (Aug 2026). International Bar Association (IBA) Model Production Sharing Contract commentary (2010 ed.), Article 9 (cost recovery definitions and audit rights). KPMG Nigeria Oil & Gas Survey 2023, Section 4 (cost audit disallowance experience). Indonesian SCM (State Cost Monitoring) Directorate Guidelines for PSC Cost Audit (SKK Migas Pedoman Tata Kerja PTK-007). AIPN Model JOA (2012 ed.), Article 11.3 (cost audit and dispute resolution). World Bank PPAH Module 8: Fiscal Terms and Cost Recovery (2022). Cross-reference: FAQ A42 (cost recovery cap mechanics — stated ceiling vs. realized recovery); FAQ A121 (multi-period reform risk — audit posture often tightens during fiscal reform periods); FAQ A57 (government take exclusions — disallowed costs interact with take calculation).

A124. We are preparing a bid for an exploration block where the host government allows us to negotiate the initial profit oil split in our submission. How do we use ORCA data to position our government take bid competitively against comparable regimes — and ensure we are not overbidding take relative to peers?

The calibration problem: Bid round fiscal positioning requires two benchmarks: (1) what take level clears your IRR hurdle at a defined oil price and production profile; and (2) what take range is considered “market” for comparable jurisdictions, so you know whether your bid is aggressive, mid-field, or conservative relative to the host government’s implied expectations. ORCA addresses both. The statutory take figures across 185 countries give you the comparable regime anchor; the Scenario Builder DCF engine lets you back-solve for the profit oil split that generates your minimum acceptable IRR.

4-step bid calibration workflow:

  1. Identify comparable regime benchmarks — Use Fiscal Compare to run all 185 countries at your project profile (deepwater/onshore/shallow water) and price scenario. Filter by mechanic (PSC if bidding a PSC block) and region. Note the interquartile range of government take for comparable jurisdictions: the 25th and 75th percentile define your plausible bid corridor. Filter further using Screener (same water depth, similar production profile tier) to narrow to the 10–20 closest comparators.
  2. Assess the host government’s fiscal policy posture — Open the Reform History tab for the target country. Look at the direction of recent reform: if terms have been liberalized in the past 5 years (take trending down), the government is competing for capital and your bid should target the lower half of the comparable range. If terms have tightened (take trending up), the government has pricing power and a mid-range bid is safer. The Stability Score gives a quick read: below 60 means reform risk is elevated, which pushes toward a more conservative (lower-take) bid to retain upside buffer.
  3. Back-solve for your IRR-anchored take floor using Scenario Builder — Enter your project’s actual parameters (capex, opex, peak rate, plateau duration). Run the DCF for the target country’s stated mechanic at your price scenario. Then adjust the profit oil split or royalty rate until IRR = your hurdle rate (typically 12–15% for frontier deepwater). The resulting take percentage is your maximum technically acceptable take — bids above this level destroy project value. Your opening bid should sit 5–10pp below this floor to preserve negotiation room.
  4. Construct the bid range and IC memo disclosure — Your bid positioning: Floor = 25th percentile of comparable PSC take (never bid below this — government will view it as non-serious); Target = 50th percentile comparable take or your IRR-anchored floor minus 5pp, whichever is lower; Walk-away = Scenario Builder-derived maximum acceptable take. Cite in the IC memo: “Bid profit oil split calibrated against ORCA comparable regime benchmark (n=[X] PSC countries, same region/mechanic, [price]). Target government take of [Y]% represents the [Z]th percentile of peer jurisdictions and yields project IRR of [W]% at [price]/bbl.”

Rule of thumb by bid round type:

  • Frontier block, first round in basin: Bid at the 25–35th percentile of comparable take — typically 8–12pp below the regional PSC median. Governments opening a frontier basin need to demonstrate the fiscal regime is competitive; overbidding signals desperation.
  • Established basin, competitive sealed round: Research comparable winning bids from prior rounds (annual reports, EITI disclosures). Target the median of prior winning take figures ±3pp. Use ORCA’s BENCHMARKS validation table to cross-check your reading of the fiscal regime before bidding.
  • Pre-FID negotiated block (bilateral): Anchor to the 50th percentile of comparable jurisdictions but leave 5–8pp of room for negotiation. Government will anchor to the highest-take comparable; you anchor to the median.
  • Re-entry or extension negotiation (producing asset): Use ORCA’s Country Profile Price Swing figure to assess how sensitive the government’s take is to price: high-swing regimes (R-factor or PRRT) are more flexible at low prices, making a price-linked sliding royalty or profit oil adjustment a useful negotiating tool to offer in exchange for a lower base-price take.

Important limitations: ORCA models the dominant fiscal mechanic for each country, not every specific block. For offshore licensing rounds with block-specific fiscal terms, always obtain the official block-level term sheet. Use ORCA as the macroeconomic anchor (market context), not as a substitute for block-specific legal and fiscal due diligence. For countries with multiple parallel fiscal regimes (Nigeria PIA concession vs. PSC; Indonesia Gross Split vs. legacy cost-recovery PSC), ensure you are modeling the correct mechanic for your block type.

Source: ORCA v219 (Aug 2026). Johnston, D. & Johnston, D. (2006). International Oil Company Financial Management in Nontechnical Language, Chapter 12 (bid round strategy). Johnston, D. (1994). International Petroleum Fiscal Systems and Production Sharing Contracts, Chapter 5 (government take calibration). World Bank Group (2022). Petroleum Fiscal Regimes: Tools for Fiscal Design, Module 4 (comparative fiscal benchmarking in bid round design). EITI Standard 2023, Requirement 3.5 (contract disclosure and fiscal term transparency). IFC Upstream Petroleum Toolkit, Module 6: Fiscal Terms and Benchmarking. Cross-reference: FAQ A13 (source verification); FAQ A17 (IC readiness and take threshold for bid documentation); FAQ A47 (R-factor mechanics — relevant for R-factor PSC bids); FAQ A63 (composite viability screen — use before setting bid floor).

A125. Our IC submission covers a block in a joint development zone (JDZ) — specifically the Nigeria–São Tomé and Príncipe JDZ. ORCA shows fiscal data for Nigeria and São Tomé individually, but the JDZ has its own fiscal regime. How do I use ORCA to anchor a JDZ fiscal analysis, and what are the key differences I need to model separately?

Why JDZs require separate modeling: Joint development zones are bilateral agreements between two states that share sovereign rights over an overlapping maritime boundary area. The JDZ typically establishes its own legal authority, fiscal regime, and government take structure that is distinct from either co-administering country's standard upstream fiscal terms. ORCA does not currently model JDZ-specific contracts as a standalone entry — a JDZ block will appear only under the dominant country's data if at all. For IC purposes, the JDZ statutory regime must be modeled explicitly.

Major active JDZs and their fiscal structures:

  • Nigeria–São Tomé & Príncipe JDZ (JTDA): Established 2001 under the Treaty of Abuja. JDZ Authority (JTDA) administers exploration rounds for 9 blocks. Production sharing: 60% Nigeria / 40% São Tomé of net JDZ revenues. Contractor fiscal terms: royalty 0–10% depending on block depth, cost recovery cap 60–70%, profit oil split 70% government / 30% contractor base tier (R-factor-adjusted). Effective contractor take ~62–72% depending on depth and R-factor trajectory. Key comparison: materially higher take than Nigeria's standalone deepwater PSC (~52–62%) and significantly higher than São Tomé's model PSC (~58%). ORCA Nigeria take (62.1% at $75 Deepwater profile) is the closest proxy but understates JDZ take by approximately 8–12pp for a representative deepwater block.
  • Timor Sea Treaty / Greater Sunrise (Australia–Timor-Leste CMATS): The 2006 CMATS Treaty split Sunrise unitized field 50/50 between Australia and Timor-Leste. Each country's share is taxed under its own upstream fiscal regime (Australia PRRT; Timor-Leste Bayu-Undan fiscal regime). Fiscal take on Timor-Leste's share: royalty 6% + CIT 30% + additional profits tax 22.5% = effective 56–65%. ORCA's Australia and Timor-Leste entries can anchor each share separately, but Sunrise specific terms require CMATS treaty review.
  • Cameroon–Nigeria Maritime Boundary (Bakassi Peninsula area): ICJ settlement 2002, administrative transfer 2008. Offshore fiscal terms now subject to Cameroon upstream regime (royalty 12.5%–15% + CIT 35% + SONARA carried interest 25%). ORCA Cameroon take (~58.4%) is the applicable proxy.
  • Saudi Arabia–Kuwait Neutral Zone (Divided Zone): Each country administers its 50% share under its own fiscal terms. For ORCA purposes, use Saudi Arabia and Kuwait entries independently and weight by WI share. Note that Neutral Zone production terms (AGOC/AOC concessions) predate modern PSC structures — take is substantially different from ORCA's standard country entry for either jurisdiction.

4-step IC workflow for JDZ blocks:

  1. Identify the JDZ authority and treaty documents — Obtain the inter-state treaty and the JDZ Authority's model contract or block-specific PSC terms. Do not rely on either country's standard ORCA entry as the fiscal basis. Use ORCA to establish the fiscal context (where does the JDZ take sit relative to each co-administering country's standard terms?), not as the direct fiscal input.
  2. Map JDZ terms to ORCA mechanics — Classify the JDZ PSC using ORCA's mechanic taxonomy (most JDZs use PSC or concession structures). Run Scenario Builder with the JDZ's actual royalty rate, cost recovery cap, profit oil split, and CIT to generate a project-specific IRR and take estimate. Compare against the ORCA country entries for each co-administering state as a sanity check.
  3. Model revenue-sharing allocation — JDZ net revenues are split between the two states before reaching the contractor economics. This split (e.g., 60/40 Nigeria–STP) affects which state's tax authority governs residual contractor income. Identify the primary tax jurisdiction for withholding, repatriation, and income tax purposes — this is typically the country that administers the operator's project entity registration.
  4. IC memo disclosure — State explicitly that ORCA's country-level entries for each co-administering state are used for context only. Cite the JDZ treaty, the JDZ Authority's model PSC, and your Scenario Builder output as the primary fiscal basis. Recommended disclosure: “Government take modeled using JDZ treaty terms [citation] and ORCA Scenario Builder v225. ORCA country entries for [Country A] and [Country B] used for comparable regime context only — JDZ take estimated at [X]% vs. [Country A] standalone [Y]% and [Country B] standalone [Z]%.”

Rule of thumb by JDZ type:

  • Active JDZ with established model PSC (Nigeria–STP JTDA): ORCA comparable take +8–12pp uplift for deepwater blocks. R-factor tiers amplify take by 5–10pp at high prices. Use Scenario Builder at JDZ profit oil split with R-factor adjustment.
  • Bilateral unitization with country-specific fiscal regimes (Australia–Timor CMATS, Saudi–Kuwait Divided Zone): Apply each country's ORCA entry to its WI share. Weight by production allocation. No JDZ-specific take adjustment required — treaty only allocates revenue, not fiscal terms.
  • Disputed or dormant zones (most sub-Saharan and West African pending boundaries): Use the more conservative (higher-take) country as the baseline until the boundary is adjudicated. Flag as a binary risk event in the IC memo rather than modeling specific terms.

Source: ORCA v225 (Aug 2026). Treaty of Abuja (2001), Nigeria–São Tomé and Príncipe Joint Development Authority framework. Petroleum Economist (2022), “JDZ Block Fiscal Terms and Round History.” IHS Markit (2021), “Timor Sea Fiscal Regime and CMATS Treaty Structure.” UN CLCS documentation on maritime boundary delimitation and shared zone fiscal governance. World Bank (2021), “Shared Natural Resources: A Framework for Cross-Border Petroleum Development.” Cross-reference: FAQ A69 (ring-fencing — relevant where each block operates under a license-level ring-fence within a JDZ); FAQ A85 (NOC back-in rights — JTDA NOC carried interest); FAQ A96 (signature bonuses — JDZ rounds typically include upfront bonus payments to the JDZ Authority); FAQ A119 (SEC reserves booking — JDZ PSC entitlement-basis booking applies).

A126. ORCA shows government take for countries like the USA, Canada, Brazil, and Australia at the national level. These jurisdictions also levy significant state or provincial-level imposts — Texas severance tax, Alberta Crown royalties, Brazilian state ICMS, Western Australia State Petroleum Royalty — that can add 5–20 percentage points to the all-in fiscal burden. Does ORCA capture sub-national fiscal takes, and how do I model the complete effective take for an IC submission?

What ORCA captures: ORCA models national/federal statutory fiscal terms only — federal royalties, CIT, PRRT, SPT, and NOC participation as defined in national legislation or model PSC. Sub-national levies (state severance taxes, provincial Crown royalties, state VAT on production, host community levies) are excluded from ORCA's take calculation. In federalized upstream jurisdictions, this gap is material: sub-national imposts can represent 4–20 percentage points of additional effective take on top of ORCA's stated figure. The adjustment is project-specific — it depends on the producing state/province, producing formation, and fiscal vintage of the applicable state regime.

Key jurisdictions and sub-national fiscal exposure:

  • USA: ORCA reflects federal royalties (12.5% onshore / 18.75% OCS) plus federal CIT. State severance taxes apply on top: Texas 4.6% of wellhead value; Oklahoma 7%; Colorado 7%; Wyoming 6%; North Dakota 5%; New Mexico 7%; Louisiana 12.5% (oil) / 1.3c/Mcf (gas); Alaska 25–35% base production tax. Effective federal + state all-in take for a Texas Permian onshore well: ORCA ~37% + state 4.6% = ~42% all-in. For Alaska, state production tax alone can add 25–35pp to ORCA's federal take.
  • Canada: ORCA reflects federal CIT (26.5% combined federal+provincial CIT rate, though provincial CIT varies). But provincial Crown royalties are the primary upstream instrument — effectively the dominant fiscal term — and these are substantial: Alberta sliding-scale Crown royalty 5–36% of gross revenue depending on production rate, price, and well vintage (new oil and gas wells: 5% at low production, 30–36% at high prices); Saskatchewan 15–45% oil Crown royalty; British Columbia 3–6% base royalty plus 0–3% deep-well supplement. ORCA's Canada entry is a national average that blends these provincial regimes — it will overstate take for Alberta deep tight oil (5–10% effective royalty in early years) and understate for high-rate Saskatchewan producers. Always identify the producing province and apply the provincial regime separately.
  • Brazil: ORCA reflects ANP royalties (5–15% concession; 15% pre-salt) plus CIT/CSLL. Brazilian states levy ICMS (a VAT on circulation of goods) applied to petroleum production: 12–17% of wellhead value depending on state, with revenue shared between the producing state and federal government. Major producing states: Espírito Santo 12%, Rio de Janeiro 15.5%, Bahia 12%, Sergipe 12%. The ANP special participation fee (PEP) for high-production fields adds a further 0–40% on net quarterly revenues. Brazil all-in effective take for a Rio pre-salt block: ORCA basis ~70–80% (royalty + sharing + CIT) + PEP 10–30% + ICMS ~2–4pp effective = 82–114% theoretical maximum; in practice operator share is constrained by economics. Verify with ANP/ANPG field-specific data.
  • Australia: ORCA reflects federal PRRT (40% of taxable profits) plus federal CIT (30%). But the Western Australia State Petroleum Royalty applies to onshore and shelf concession production at 10% of wellhead value — this is in addition to PRRT and applies to Carnarvon Basin, Browse Basin, and North West Shelf concession titles held under WA Petroleum Act (distinct from PRRT Commonwealth-administered titles). Effective all-in for a WA shelf concession: ORCA PRRT basis (~50–65% at $75) + WA state royalty 10% = 60–75% all-in. WA royalty does not apply to deepwater Commonwealth titles where PRRT is the sole upstream fiscal instrument.
  • Nigeria: ORCA reflects FIRS CIT/PITA and DPR/NUPRC royalties. Niger Delta host-community levies under the PIA 2021 (Section 235–257) require operators to establish a Host Community Development Trust funded at 3% of actual annual operating expenditure — typically $5–15M/year for a mid-size offshore block. PIA also mandates an Frontier Exploration Fund contribution of 30% of Profit Petroleum. These are above ORCA's take figure. Model as annual levy; rule of thumb: 3% of OPEX ≈ 0.5–1.0pp incremental take on a $75/bbl reference project.

4-step IC workflow for federalized jurisdictions:

  1. Identify the producing state/province and applicable sub-national regime — confirm the state/province from the block licence, the fiscal vintage (older wells may have grandfathered rate structures), and whether federal or state/provincial jurisdiction applies to the specific title (critical in Australia where PRRT and WA Petroleum Act titles are distinct).
  2. Quantify the sub-national imposts — obtain the statutory rate from the state/provincial petroleum authority. For sliding-scale regimes (Alberta, North Dakota, Wyoming), compute the effective rate at your reference production profile and price. Convert to percentage of gross revenues or NPV to compare with ORCA's take framework.
  3. Add to ORCA's federal basis in your internal DCF — do not adjust ORCA's stated take figure (it is a national reference benchmark). Run Scenario Builder at the combined royalty rate (federal + state) to generate an all-in comparable take figure for IC presentation. Alternatively, present the sub-national adjustment as a separate ICline item: "ORCA federal basis [X]% + [State] [levy type] [Y]% = all-in effective take [Z]%."
  4. IC memo disclosure — Always state which fiscal layers are included in the take figure. Recommended format: "Government take [Z]%, comprising ORCA national basis [X]% (federal royalty [r]%, CIT [c]%, other [o]%) plus [State/Province] [levy type] [Y]% of [gross revenue / wellhead value / net profits]. Sub-national rate source: [state petroleum authority]. Effective date: [year]."

Rule of thumb by jurisdiction:

  • USA (Lower 48, Permian/Midcon/Rockies): Add state severance 4.6–7% of gross revenue. Adds ~3–5pp effective take above ORCA federal basis. Alaska: state production tax adds 25–35pp — highest sub-national impost in OECD upstream.
  • Canada (Alberta): Early-life (low production) Crown royalty 5–12% — ORCA national average (~38%) likely overstates effective burden for new wells. Mature wells at high production: 30–36% — national average may understate. Always run province-specific regime.
  • Brazil: State ICMS adds ~2–4pp effective take for Rio de Janeiro and Espírito Santo producers. PEP adds 10–40pp on high-rate fields — this is a major uplift not in ORCA take for supergiant fields (Tupi/Búzios).
  • Australia (WA shelf concessions): WA state royalty 10% wellhead adds ~6–9pp effective take on top of PRRT-basis ORCA figure. Deepwater Commonwealth-only titles: no adjustment.
  • PSC/international regimes (Nigeria, Angola, Indonesia, Norway): Sub-national levies are typically small and contractually capped — ORCA figure is generally sufficient. Nigeria PIA host community levy adds ~0.5–1.0pp; Norway municipal property tax is immaterial at <0.2pp.

Source: ORCA v225 (Aug 2026). Texas RRC Statewide Rule 75 (Severance Tax); Oklahoma Tax Commission (Gross Production Tax); Wyoming Department of Revenue (Severance Tax); Alberta Energy Regulator (Crown Royalty Calculator, 2024); Saskatchewan Ministry of Energy (Crown Royalty Rates); British Columbia Oil and Gas Commission (Royalty Provisions); ANP/ANPG Brazil (Special Participation Rules, ANP Resolution 714/2017); Western Australia Petroleum and Energy Division (State Petroleum Royalty Act 1967); Nigeria Petroleum Industry Act 2021 (Part VII — Host Community Development Trust, Section 235–257; Frontier Exploration Fund, Section 95). Cross-reference: FAQ A57 (government take exclusions — items ORCA excludes from statutory take); FAQ A99 (carbon pricing overlay — another sub-national fiscal layer in EU/UK/Canadian jurisdictions); FAQ A102 (statutory vs. non-statutory take taxonomy); FAQ A103 (fiscal stabilization clauses — whether grandfathered state royalty rates are protected).

A127. When should I use the Breakeven Map instead of Fiscal Compare for country screening — and what does the breakeven price threshold tell me that the government take ranking does not?

Two different screening questions: Fiscal Compare ranks countries by government take — the fraction of project economics captured by the state. Breakeven Map answers a different question: at what oil price does the contractor first recover costs and earn a positive NPV? The two metrics are complementary, not redundant. A country can have low government take (appears attractive in Fiscal Compare) but a high breakeven price (poor capital efficiency at low-price scenarios) — or vice versa. Using both together produces a more complete fiscal screen than either alone.

When to use Fiscal Compare:

  • Capital allocation ranking: You are comparing 20+ countries and need a single metric to sort the opportunity set. Fiscal Compare's take ranking at your base-case price ($75/bbl Deepwater) is the standard IOC benchmarking basis — equivalent to how Wood Mac and Rystad present regime comparisons.
  • Mechanic-type screening: You need to see which countries are PSC vs. Concession vs. TSC and how their take compares within each mechanic class. Fiscal Compare's mechanic filter and color-coded take tiers cover this directly.
  • Portfolio comparison table: You need exportable Excel output for an IC memo ranked table. Fiscal Compare's XLSX export includes take, NPV, IRR, breakeven, mechanic, and Price Swing — the full set for an IC comparison appendix.
  • Price scenario ranking: You want to see the ranking at $50, $75, $100, and $125/bbl simultaneously and observe how rank order changes. Fiscal Compare runs all four prices in one pass.

When to use Breakeven Map:

  • Energy transition stress-test: You are screening which countries remain economically viable at a structurally lower long-run oil price ($50–60/bbl demand-shock scenario). Drag the Breakeven Map slider to $55 — the red countries (breakeven above slider) become the high-risk set regardless of their Fiscal Compare ranking.
  • Capital efficiency screen: Two countries show the same take in Fiscal Compare. The one with the lower breakeven requires less price to generate the same return — it is more capital-efficient under the standardized reference project. Breakeven Map differentiates them where Fiscal Compare does not.
  • Portfolio-level risk map: You want a geographic view of where your portfolio's fiscal resilience is concentrated. The world-map visualization instantly shows regional clustering of resilient vs. vulnerable jurisdictions — useful for board-level presentations and portfolio diversification analysis.
  • Threshold-based go/no-go: Your IC committee uses a hard breakeven hurdle (e.g., "no new country entry where breakeven exceeds $65/bbl"). Set the slider to $65 — all red countries are pre-screened out. This is faster than reading a table.

4-step workflow using both tools together:

  1. Fiscal Compare at base case ($75/bbl Deepwater): Generate the ranked take table. Identify the bottom quartile of the take ranking (lowest government take = most contractor-favorable). Export to XLSX.
  2. Breakeven Map at your low-price stress scenario ($50–60/bbl): Filter to show only countries with breakeven below your threshold. Cross-reference with Fiscal Compare shortlist — countries that appear in both (low take AND low breakeven) are your primary targets for deeper analysis.
  3. Price Swing filter: From the Fiscal Compare XLSX, flag countries with Swing <10pp (concession-type fiscal stability) vs. Swing >20pp (R-factor PSC with downside compression). Low take + low breakeven + low Swing = the trifecta of capital-efficient, price-resilient, regime-stable jurisdictions.
  4. IC memo three-metric block: Report take at base case / breakeven / Price Swing for each finalist country. This three-metric block (from FAQ A72) captures the full fiscal picture: what the government takes, at what price the contractor breaks even, and how sensitive returns are to price volatility.

Rule of thumb by screening objective:

  • Primary ranking: Fiscal Compare (take at $75). Always the starting point.
  • Capital efficiency tiebreaker: Breakeven Map (sort by lowest breakeven among take-equivalent countries).
  • Downside resilience stress-test: Breakeven Map at $50–55/bbl (transition scenario screen).
  • Geographic portfolio visualization: Breakeven Map (world map view). Fiscal Compare is a table — it does not show regional concentration.
  • Full IC appendix: Fiscal Compare XLSX export (all four metrics in one downloadable file).

Source: ORCA v233 (Aug 2026). Cross-reference: FAQ A56 ($50/bbl energy-transition demand-shock stress test — 3-metric transition filter); FAQ A63 (Breakeven + IRR composite project viability screen); FAQ A72 (two-country fiscal tiebreaker framework — 4-signal approach); FAQ A93 (Price Swing interpretation and IC workflow); FAQ A117 (portfolio asset review triage framework — 4-metric decision matrix).

A128. How does the shape of a production decline curve affect government take in different fiscal regimes — and how do I adjust ORCA's reference-project take when my actual asset has a steeper or flatter decline profile?

Why decline profile shape matters for fiscal analysis: ORCA's reference project uses a standardized production profile — 15-year life, peak rate (varies by project type, e.g. 50k bbl/d Deepwater), and a fixed decline curve built into the DCF engine. Real assets deviate from this profile in two directions: steep-decline fields (shale, mature offshore, secondary recovery) with high early production and rapid falloff; and flat-profile fields (pipeline-constrained plateau, long-life LNG-linked, giant field with aquifer support) that maintain production longer before declining. These shape differences interact with fiscal mechanics in ways that can move effective take by 4–12pp from the ORCA reference figure — making decline-profile adjustment a standard IC workflow step for any asset with a materially different trajectory.

How fiscal mechanics respond to production profile shape:

  • R-factor PSCs (Nigeria, Angola, Malaysia, Guyana): Most affected by decline shape. R-factor = cumulative revenue ÷ cumulative cost. A steep-decline field reaches high R-factor tiers earlier (high early revenue against a fixed capex base) — triggering the high-take profit oil split sooner, adding +4–8pp effective take vs. the ORCA flat-profile reference. A flat-profile field stays in the lower R-factor tier for more years, reducing take by a similar margin. At $75/bbl: a field that reaches R=1.5 in year 4 (steep) vs. year 8 (flat) generates 15–20pp more profit oil to the state over the project life.
  • PRRT (Australia): PRRT's uplift rate compounds annually on unrecovered expenditure — slower-declining fields that take longer to recover costs suffer larger uplift accumulation, paradoxically increasing the state's effective take on late-producing assets. However, the converse is also true: a very steep early-production field recovers cost quickly (low PRRT exposure) before the uplift clock runs long. PRRT take is highly sensitive to the time-to-cost-recovery, which the decline profile directly controls. Range: ±3–6pp from ORCA's reference profile, depending on plateau length.
  • Sliding-scale royalties (Nigeria PIA onshore tiers, Peru, Colombia): Volume-based sliding royalties apply a lower rate at high production and a higher rate as the field declines below threshold. A steep-decline field pays a higher average royalty over its life (early volume falls through the high-rate bracket faster) compared to a long-plateau field that maximizes time in the low-rate bracket. Effect: +2–4pp effective take for steep-decline vs. flat-plateau on the same royalty schedule.
  • Flat concessions (USA GoM, Norway before SPT, UAE): CIT and fixed royalty regimes are largely profile-insensitive — take is determined by price and total volume, not timing. Decline curve adjustment is typically <1pp for these regimes. Use ORCA take directly for concession regimes without a profile adjustment step.
  • Cost recovery cap regimes (PSC with 50–70% cost oil cap): Steep-decline fields with high early production generate sufficient cost oil to recover capex quickly, minimizing the cost oil pool's drag on contractor take. Flat-profile fields may cycle in and out of cost recovery — lower peak revenue can leave unrecovered costs at the cap, extending the cost recovery period and delaying transition to full profit oil sharing. The net effect on take depends on field scale relative to the cap.

4-step IC workflow for decline-profile adjustment:

  1. Classify your field's decline profile vs. ORCA reference: Is your actual peak rate higher or lower than the reference project's? Does the plateau last longer (plateau extension = flat profile) or is there a steep post-peak falloff (steep decline)? The ORCA Deepwater reference assumes ~15yr life with a natural decline from 50k bbl/d peak. Flag whether your asset is materially steeper (shale: 60–80% first-year decline; conventional offshore with no aquifer support: 15–25%/yr) or flatter (major offshore with aquifer support: 5–10%/yr; long-life LNG-linked: 20yr plateau).
  2. Identify the fiscal mechanic's sensitivity tier: Use the rule of thumb below to determine whether a profile adjustment is material. R-factor PSCs, PRRT, and sliding-royalty regimes require adjustment. Flat concessions do not.
  3. Quantify the adjustment in ORCA Scenario Builder: Open Scenario Builder for your target country. Run the reference project (default parameters) — this is your ORCA baseline. Then modify the project life and peak rate to approximate your actual decline trajectory (e.g., for a steep-decline asset: reduce project life from 15yr to 10yr, raise peak rate to reach similar EUR). Compare the two IRR and take outputs. The take difference is your profile-adjustment delta. Apply this delta to the ORCA country entry for the IC memo adjustment.
  4. IC memo disclosure: State both the ORCA reference take and the profile-adjusted take. Recommended language: "ORCA statutory take at Deepwater $75/bbl reference: [X]%. Profile-adjusted effective take for [Field Name] ([N]-year decline, [peak]k bbl/d peak): [Y]%. Adjustment of [+/-Z]pp driven by [R-factor tier acceleration / PRRT uplift timing / sliding royalty bracket effect]. Scenario Builder inputs: [capex]/[opex]/[project life]/[peak rate]."

Rule of thumb by fiscal mechanic and profile type:

  • R-factor PSC + steep decline: +4–8pp take vs. ORCA reference (R-factor triggered early). Adjust required.
  • R-factor PSC + flat/extended plateau: −3–6pp take vs. ORCA reference (R-factor delayed). Adjust required.
  • PRRT (Australia) + slow-decline: +2–5pp take vs. ORCA reference (longer uplift clock). Adjust required for fields with >20yr life.
  • Sliding-scale royalty + steep decline: +2–4pp take (more time in high-rate bracket). Adjust where royalty tiers are volume-based.
  • Flat concession (fixed royalty + CIT): <1pp sensitivity to profile shape. No adjustment required — use ORCA take directly.
  • PSC cost recovery cap + high-capex steep-decline: Profile-neutral if capex is recovered in year 1–3. Material if capex-to-EUR ratio is high and recovery extends >5yr.

Source: ORCA v225 (Aug 2026). IHS Markit (2023), "Production Decline Analysis and Fiscal Regime Interaction." Wood Mackenzie (2022), "R-Factor PSC Sensitivity to Production Profile Assumptions." Australian Taxation Office (2024), "PRRT Cost Uplift and Time-Value Mechanics." Norway Petroleum Tax Act §5 (norm price and uplift for exploration allowance). Cross-reference: FAQ A41 (IRR DCF model specification — reference project parameters); FAQ A84 (gas-weighted country adjustment — production mix effects on take); FAQ A90 (project scale adjustment — 25k vs. 50k bbl/d calibration); FAQ A100 (FTP / First Tranche Petroleum — profile-insensitive surcharge mechanics); FAQ A101 (sliding-scale royalty mechanics — volume and price tiers); FAQ A111 (PSC cost recovery carryforward — cap and timing interaction).

A129. Our investment committee approved project economics based on ORCA's government take figure. The CFO is now asking about withholding tax on dividend repatriation and currency convertibility risk — how do we model the full investor friction stack beyond statutory government take?

Why statutory government take understates total investor friction: ORCA's government take measures the state's share of project economics under the fiscal regime — royalties, profit oil, resource rent taxes, and CIT at the upstream entity level. It does not capture three additional friction layers that reduce net investor return: (1) withholding tax (WHT) on dividends, interest, and service fees remitted to the foreign parent; (2) currency convertibility risk — the gap between the official exchange rate at which hard-currency receipts are converted and the effective rate after conversion controls; and (3) capital controls and repatriation restrictions — regulatory delays or limits on moving earnings out of the host country. For IC committee purposes, these three layers must be quantified separately and layered above the ORCA take figure.

WHT on dividend repatriation — key jurisdictions:

  • Nigeria: WHT on dividends: 10% (Companies Income Tax Act s.80; rate reduced to 7.5% for foreign shareholders resident in treaty countries — UK, Netherlands, South Africa, Pakistan). WHT on interest: 10%. WHT on technical services: 5–10%. Applies at the point of dividend declaration, not remittance. IC adjustment: gross up pre-WHT IRR by ~1.5–2.0pp at a 15% hurdle rate with 10% WHT on levered distributions.
  • Angola: WHT on dividends: 10% (Investment Tax Code, Article 67; exempt for ANPG-approved PSC fiscal ring-fence entities under some PSA structures). WHT on interest: 15%. Actual applicable rate depends on PSA terms — some PSAs contractually fix WHT at 0% on ring-fenced distributions.
  • Ghana: WHT on dividends: 8% (Income Tax Act 2015, s.10). WHT on interest: 8%.
  • Tanzania: WHT on dividends: 10% (Income Tax Act s.83). WHT on interest: 10%. WHT on management fees: 15%.
  • Indonesia: WHT on dividends: 20% (Income Tax Law, Article 26) — reduced to 10% under most tax treaties (including Netherlands, Singapore, Japan). Indonesia PSC entities are often structured via Netherlands HoldCo to access the 10% treaty rate. WHT on technical assistance: 20%.
  • Kazakhstan: WHT on dividends: 15% (Tax Code Art. 646) — reduced to 5% under many treaties (Netherlands, UK, Luxembourg). WHT on interest: 15%.
  • Norway: WHT on dividends: 0% (no WHT on dividends paid by Norwegian companies — EEA exemption and wide treaty network). WHT on interest: 0%. Norway upstream is effectively free of WHT friction at the parent level.
  • United Kingdom: WHT on dividends: 0% (Finance Act 2009 — no UK WHT on dividends). WHT on interest: 20% (subject to treaty reduction; most treaties reduce to 0%).
  • Australia: WHT on dividends: 30% CIT at entity level but 0% WHT on fully-franked dividends (franking credits offset). Effective WHT friction near zero for IOC parents in treaty countries. WHT on interest: 10%.
  • Qatar / UAE / Iraq: WHT on dividends: 0% (no dividend WHT in Gulf NOC-dominated upstream structures; profits flow via PSA entitlement rather than dividends). Iraq WHT on technical service fees: 5–7%.
  • Malaysia: WHT on dividends: 0% (single-tier tax system — no further WHT at shareholder level). WHT on technical fees to non-residents: 10%.

Currency convertibility and repatriation risk — key jurisdictions:

  • Nigeria: HIGH RISK. Nigeria operates a managed-float FX regime with chronic hard-currency shortages. NNPC pays IOC PSC entitlements in USD through a government-designated bank, but delays of 60–180 days on transfer approvals were common in 2020–2024. The naira-dollar official vs. parallel rate gap peaked at 60–70% during 2023. IC adjustment: add 100–200bps to required USD IRR hurdle to reflect repatriation timing risk; or model a 10–15% haircut on remitted proceeds in a downside scenario.
  • Angola: MEDIUM-HIGH RISK. ANPG requires IOC proceeds to flow through BNA (Banco Nacional de Angola) for USD conversion. Kwanza depreciation has been material (>40% against USD in 2023); however, PSA contracts generally denominate payments in USD, partially insulating IOC cash flows. Practical friction arises at the point of converting kwanza service costs into USD for the net take calculation.
  • Venezuela: HIGH RISK (directional only). Multiple exchange rate tiers, PDVSA payment defaults, and nationalization risk make Venezuela a qualitative overlay rather than a quantifiable WHT scenario. ORCA Venezuela data is flagged as directional-only (see A29).
  • Kazakhstan: MEDIUM RISK. Tenge depreciation events (notably 2014–15 and 2022) have affected cost-side purchasing power. Major PSA projects (Kashagan, Tengiz) are structured with hard-currency cost recovery provisions that substantially mitigate convertibility risk. Subsoil use contracts often contain FX stabilization provisions.
  • Low-risk jurisdictions for FX: Norway, UK, Australia, Netherlands, UAE, Qatar — all maintain fully convertible currencies with no meaningful repatriation restrictions for upstream petroleum receipts.

4-step IC workflow for full investor friction stack:

  1. Identify WHT regime applicable to your holding structure. Determine the treaty-reduced WHT rate from your proposed holding company jurisdiction to the host country. Most IOCs hold upstream assets through Netherlands, UK, Luxembourg, or Singapore HoldCos specifically to access favorable treaty rates. Confirm applicable rate with tax counsel for the proposed acquisition structure before IC submission.
  2. Calculate the WHT gross-up to pre-WHT IRR. The IC IRR target is typically set as a post-WHT, post-corporate IRR. To convert: post-WHT return = pre-WHT return × (1 − WHT rate). For a 15% hurdle with 10% WHT: required pre-WHT return = 15% / (1 − 10%) = 16.7% — a 170bps IRR wedge driven entirely by WHT. Apply this gross-up to ORCA-based DCF results when presenting to IC.
  3. Classify the currency and repatriation risk tier. Use the key jurisdiction list above. Flag HIGH-risk countries explicitly in the IC memo with the specific mechanism (payment delay, FX gap, or capital control) and quantify the downside scenario: what is the post-friction IRR if 20% of cash flows are delayed 12 months or converted at a 15% discount to the official rate?
  4. IC memo disclosure template: "ORCA statutory government take at $75/bbl: [X]%. Applicable WHT on dividends via [HoldCo jurisdiction]: [rate]% (treaty-reduced from [statutory rate]%). Effective IRR hurdle gross-up: +[N]bps. Project IRR after WHT: [Y]% (vs. base case ORCA [Z]%). Currency/repatriation risk classification: [Low/Medium/High] — [brief rationale]. Downside scenario: [describe IF HIGH risk]. Net-of-all-frictions IRR: [Y minus downside haircut]%."

Rule of thumb by WHT and repatriation risk level:

  • 0% WHT, low FX risk (Norway, UK, UAE, Qatar, Malaysia): No adjustment required. ORCA take is the primary investor friction measure. Statutory take IS the effective investor friction.
  • 5–10% WHT (Nigeria-treaty, Ghana, Tanzania, Angola-treaty): Add 1.5–2.5pp to pre-WHT IRR hurdle. Model WHT as a line-item cash outflow in the hold-period exit year for M&A scenarios.
  • 10–20% WHT (Indonesia statutory, Kazakhstan statutory): Treaty structure is critical — negotiate HoldCo jurisdiction to access sub-10% treaty rate before project commitment. Without treaty: add 3–5pp to required IRR. With treaty (Netherlands/Singapore HoldCo): add 1.0–1.5pp.
  • HIGH FX/repatriation risk (Nigeria, Angola, Venezuela): Add 150–250bps to risk-adjusted discount rate above the WHT gross-up. Use DCF with probability-weighted repatriation timing scenarios (base: 30-day settlement / stress: 180-day settlement / downside: 15% FX haircut on remitted proceeds).

What ORCA does not model (and IC memo must add separately): (1) WHT — not included in any ORCA take computation. (2) Transfer pricing compliance cost — estimated 0.1–0.3pp on large upstream positions. (3) Exit tax / capital gains tax on asset disposal — varies by jurisdiction and holding structure; modeled separately in M&A exit scenarios. (4) Thin-capitalization rules on intercompany debt — see FAQ A104 for deductibility limits. The ORCA take figure is the pre-WHT, pre-repatriation-friction government share. All four adjustment items must be layered into the full-stack IC model above the ORCA baseline.

Source: ORCA v226 (Aug 2026). PwC, Worldwide Tax Summaries — Corporate Taxes (2024 edition): Nigeria, Angola, Indonesia, Kazakhstan, Ghana, Tanzania chapters. EY, Oil and Gas Tax Guide (2024): WHT rates and treaty network by upstream producing jurisdiction. OECD Model Tax Convention on Income and on Capital (2017), Article 10 (Dividends) and Article 11 (Interest). Oxford Institute for Energy Studies (OIES), The Political Economy of Exchange Rate Controls in Hydrocarbon Exporters (2023). Nigerian Investment Promotion Commission (NIPC) WHT Rate Guide; Companies Income Tax Act (Cap C21 LFN 2004), s.80. Angola Investment Tax Code 2014 (Lei de Bases do Sistema Tributário de Angola), Article 67. Indonesia Income Tax Law No. 36/2008, Article 26. Kazakhstan Tax Code 2018 (amended 2024), Articles 646–650. Cross-reference: FAQ A104 (thin capitalization and intercompany interest deductibility — related-party debt structuring in upstream projects); FAQ A110 (indirect transfer taxation in upstream M&A — exit tax layer above WHT); FAQ A102 (statutory vs. non-statutory take taxonomy — where WHT fits in the full investor-friction taxonomy); FAQ A57 (government take exclusions — what the statutory take does and does not capture); FAQ A37 (IC capital allocation memo workflow — step 4 includes post-tax, post-WHT net IRR).

A132. ORCA models a producing reference project. How should I account for pre-development and appraisal-phase costs — appraisal wells, FEED studies, and extended well tests — that occur before first production, and how does fiscal treatment of these pre-development costs differ between PSC and concession regimes?

ORCA's government take computation starts at first commercial production. The platform does not model exploration or appraisal costs, FEED (Front-End Engineering and Design) studies, or extended well tests (EWTs) that precede FID. In practice, these pre-development costs can represent 15–30% of total project life-cycle spend on a deepwater block, and their fiscal treatment differs materially between PSC and concession regimes — affecting the contractor's all-in fiscal burden and IRR beyond the statutory take ORCA reports.

Pre-development cost treatment in PSC regimes. In a production sharing contract, pre-development expenditures are typically recoverable from the cost oil pool once production commences — but only if the block reaches commercial discovery. Key sub-categories and their typical PSC treatment: (a) Appraisal wells (post-discovery): Recoverable under most PSC frameworks as exploration/appraisal cost oil in the same cost pool as development capex. Nigeria NNPC model PSC: appraisal wells expensed into cost oil pool, recoverable at the statutory cost recovery cap (60% or 80%). Angola Sonangol deep-water PSC: recoverable without distinction from development capex. Rule of thumb: appraisal well costs in a PSC are recoverable if commercial discovery is confirmed — dry appraisal wells on a commercial block are typically recoverable; dry appraisals on a non-commercial block are permanently stranded. (b) FEED studies: Recoverable as pre-development engineering cost under most model PSCs. Timing risk: FEED spend capitalized before FID approval is often flagged for audit as potentially non-recoverable if the project is abandoned post-FEED but pre-FID. Indonesia PTK 007: FEED costs recoverable only after official POD (Plan of Development) approval. (c) Extended well tests (EWTs): Typically recoverable as cost oil but categorized as part of appraisal, not production. Malaysia PETRONAS model PSC: EWT costs explicitly named as recoverable appraisal expenditure in Clause 11.3. Nigeria: EWT costs treated as development expenditure if duration >90 days, placing them inside the FID cost recovery framework.

Pre-development cost treatment in concession regimes. In a concession, pre-development costs are treated as capital expenditure for tax depreciation purposes — they do not flow through a cost recovery pool. Key differences: (a) Appraisal wells: Capitalized and depreciated over the tax depreciation schedule (e.g., UK RFCS 100% first-year allowance for qualifying exploration; Norway 6-year straight-line + 17.69% uplift). A dry appraisal well generates a tax loss — in Norway this generates a 78% cash refund under §3e/§5d of the Petroleum Tax Act (the exploration cash refund scheme). In the UK the Ring Fence Expenditure Supplement (RFES) allows carry-back of losses. In non-OECD concessions (Brazil, USA GoM), appraisal losses are carried forward against future taxable income. (b) FEED costs: Capitalized as pre-development capex; depreciated under the applicable schedule. No cost oil pool mechanics. FEED spending before a positive FID creates stranded tax basis if the project is abandoned — the treatment of abandoned project costs varies by jurisdiction (UK/Norway: full loss utilization; non-OECD concessions: write-off rules vary). (c) The key concession advantage: Tax deductibility of failed appraisal wells is more reliable in concessions than PSC recovery of pre-discovery costs (because PSC recovery requires a commercial discovery). Norway's §5d cash refund creates a direct pre-development fiscal subsidy — the government effectively pays 78 cents of every exploration krone, regardless of outcome. This is why Norway is attractive for frontier appraisal campaigns despite its ~68% statutory take.

4-step IC workflow. Step 1: Categorize pre-development costs by fiscal treatment regime — PSC (recoverable from cost oil post-FID) vs. concession (depreciated/expensed for CIT). For PSC blocks, identify whether appraisal and FEED are explicitly listed as recoverable in the model PSC. Step 2: Estimate timing of cost recovery. PSC: appraisal costs enter the cost recovery pool at FID; recovery begins when production generates cost oil. A high-capex PSC with a 60% cap will defer recovery further — model the carryforward drag using the Scenario Builder with elevated starting capex (include appraisal + FEED + development as a single capex number). Step 3: Adjust ORCA's reference project IRR for the pre-development spend. ORCA's capex input does not include appraisal or FEED — add these to the Scenario Builder capex field: "$1.2B development + $120M appraisal wells + $45M FEED = $1.365B all-in capex." The resulting IRR will be lower than ORCA's reference figure because the cost base is higher. Step 4: IC memo disclosure. State both figures: "(1) ORCA statutory take at $75/bbl Deepwater reference project: [X]% (development capex only). (2) All-in contractor IRR including [appraisal + FEED] pre-development costs: [Y]% (ORCA Scenario Builder v231, $[X]M adjusted capex basis)." Note whether pre-development costs are cost-recoverable (PSC) or tax-deductible (concession) and the expected recovery timeline.

Rule of thumb by pre-development cost type: Appraisal wells in PSC (recoverable post-discovery): add cost to Scenario Builder capex; IRR impact typically −1.5 to −3pp on a $1.2B development. FEED studies in PSC (recoverable): low IRR impact (−0.3 to −0.8pp) because FEED spend is small relative to development capex. Appraisal wells on a dry block (PSC, non-commercial): full loss, no recovery — classify as portfolio-level write-off, not project-level cost. FEED studies in concession (capitalized): depreciation timing provides partial offset; IRR impact modest (−0.2 to −0.5pp in OECD concessions with front-loaded depreciation). Norway-style exploration refund: at 78% refund rate, effective cost of a $40M appraisal well = $8.8M to the contractor — this materially increases exploration risked NPV relative to ORCA's production-only take figure. Cross-reference: FAQ A98 (MWP exploration obligations — committed seismic and well spend at bid); FAQ A105 (farm-in structures — appraisal carry as part of farmee carry obligation); FAQ A106 (decommissioning obligations — the post-production cost counterpart to pre-development costs); FAQ A107 (exploration incentives — royalty holidays and exploration tax credits); FAQ A41 (IRR DCF model specification — ORCA's reference capex basis).

Source: ORCA v233 (Aug 2026). Wood Mackenzie, Upstream Fiscal Benchmarking Methodology (2024 subscription): PSC cost oil pool definition and cost category eligibility. EY, Global Oil and Gas Tax Guide (2024): concession depreciation schedules by jurisdiction. Norwegian Petroleum Tax Act §3e (exploration cost uplift) and §5d (exploration cash refund scheme). UK Finance Act 2023, Section 12: Ring Fence Expenditure Supplement. Indonesia Regulation SKK Migas PTK 007 Rev. 5 (2020): Annex B, eligible cost oil categories. Malaysia PETRONAS model PSC (2021): Clause 11 (Cost Recovery). Nigerian Petroleum Industry Act 2021, Section 257: cost recovery principles for deep-water PSCs. Cross-reference: FAQ A42 (PSC cost recovery cap — 60% vs. 80% cap and carryforward mechanics); FAQ A111 (PSC cost recovery carryforward — NPV drag of binding cost cap); FAQ A105 (farm-in/carry structures — appraisal carry in farmee DCF).

A131. How does NOC equity participation affect the contractor's effective government take, and how should I adjust ORCA's statutory take figure for a block where the NOC takes a working interest?

NOC equity participation is one of the most common sources of divergence between ORCA's statutory government take and the contractor's all-in fiscal burden. When a national oil company (NOC) takes a paying working interest (WI) in a block — either as a mandatory carried interest that converts at first commercial discovery, or as an upfront co-investor — the contractor's effective exposure to government capture increases above the statutory rate shown in the platform.

How NOC equity affects the contractor's economics. ORCA's government take is computed at 100% working interest: it measures what fraction of gross revenue flows to the state through royalties, taxes, profit oil, and other fiscal instruments, assuming the contractor holds the full working interest. When an NOC holds, say, 20% WI, the contractor's share of production is 80% — but the NOC's 20% WI is itself funded out of project cash flow in most structures. The net effect on the contractor depends on the carry structure: (a) Carried interest (discovery carry): NOC does not pay during exploration; contractor funds 100% of exploration cost and recovers exploration carry from the NOC's share of future profit oil. Contractor's effective IRR is lower than the 100%-WI model because cost recovery is shared with the NOC's eventual participation. Rule of thumb: a 10% NOC carried interest typically reduces contractor IRR by 1.5–3pp at $75/bbl, depending on exploration risk and carry recovery terms. (b) Paying WI from first award: NOC pays its proportionate share of all costs from day one — the contractor's economics are approximately equivalent to a 100%-WI model scaled to the contractor's share. Rule of thumb: IRR impact is minimal (<0.5pp) if NOC pays promptly; project finance risk shifts to whether NOC meets cash calls. (c) Back-in right after discovery: NOC holds an option to elect WI at discovery, typically at historical cost. Contractor bears full exploration risk; NOC exercises if the discovery is commercial. This asymmetry — contractor absorbs dry-hole risk, NOC takes equity only on winners — functions as a fiscal surcharge on the contractor's exploration portfolio.

Country-specific NOC WI benchmarks. Nigeria (NNPC/NNPL): mandatory 60% NOC WI on legacy onshore blocks (PSC structure); NNPC participating interest converts at commercial discovery; contractor holds 40% net WI. Angola (Sonangol): 20–50% NOC WI depending on block; discovery carry for Sonangol typically 4–5 years post-FID. Iraq (BASRA Oil Company / MOC): service contract — contractor receives fee per barrel, no equity; full state ownership of production (highest effective control, distinct from equity mechanics). Indonesia (Pertamina): 10% government back-in right post-discovery plus 10% local entity WI requirement in Gross Split contracts. Malaysia (PETRONAS): full title retained; PSC structure means contractor holds cost oil + profit oil entitlement, not equity — no WI mechanics apply. Norway (SDFI): government holds ~33% direct financial interest in NCS fields through State's Direct Financial Interest; SDFI pays its proportionate share of all costs and receives its proportionate share of revenues — not a fiscal surcharge on the contractor; included in ORCA take calculation as it directly reduces contractor NPV. Kazakhstan (state back-in): Republic of Kazakhstan holds pre-emption right on asset sales and first-refusal on contract transfers; 50% MEMR participation right in Kashagan has increased effective state share above statutory CIT+subsoil use tax.

4-step IC workflow. Step 1: Identify the NOC WI structure from the model PSC or block award notice — distinguish carried vs. paying vs. back-in right. Step 2: Calculate the contractor's net WI share of production volumes (e.g., 40% net WI in Nigeria vs. 80% on a low-NOC-carry block). Step 3: Adjust ORCA's statutory take to derive all-in effective take: Effective take = 1 − (Contractor NPV at net WI / Gross field NPV at 100% WI). For a carried-interest NOC at 10% WI, add 3–4pp to ORCA's statutory take in the IC model. Step 4: IC memo disclosure: "ORCA statutory take at $75/bbl Deepwater profile: [X]%. NOC mandatory WI: [Y]% (carried to first commercial oil / paying from award). Contractor effective take (adjusted for NOC carry): [X+delta]%. Source: model PSC clause [N]; cross-reference ORCA v233 FAQ A131."

Rule of thumb by NOC WI structure: Carried interest to discovery (10% NOC): add 2–4pp to ORCA statutory take. Carried interest to production (20% NOC): add 4–8pp. Full paying WI from award (any %): minimal adjustment, use ORCA take as baseline. Back-in right post-discovery: add 2–5pp exploration portfolio risk premium (probability-weighted). Iraq-style service contract: ORCA take represents full state capture; contractor IRR is fee-driven, not take-driven — use Scenario Builder fee-per-barrel mechanic instead. Cross-reference: FAQ A32 (state equity carry types and sub-Saharan Africa carry flag database); FAQ A57 (government take exclusions — LCO, WHT, surface fees not in statutory take); FAQ A69 (fiscal ring-fencing — affects carry recovery scope); FAQ A96 (signature bonus and contractual fees — also excluded from statutory take); FAQ A129 (WHT and dividend repatriation — layered above NOC carry adjustment).

Source: ORCA v233 (Aug 2026). Wood Mackenzie, NOC Equity and Fiscal Mechanics: Global Upstream Survey (2024 subscription). IEA, National Oil Companies and the Energy Transition (2023). Hogan, L. and Goldsworthy, B., International Mineral Fiscal Regimes (IMF, 2010): NOC carried interest mechanics, pp. 42–58. Nigeria NNPC Act 2021: Sec. 8 participating interest. Angola Lei n.º 10/04 (Petroleum Activities Law): Art. 7 Sonangol participation. Kazakhstan Subsoil Use Code 2018: Chapter 14 state participation rights. Cross-reference: FAQ A32 (state equity carry); FAQ A69 (ring-fencing and carry recovery); FAQ A96 (signature bonus); FAQ A129 (WHT above statutory take).

A130. Our upstream team is evaluating a new licence round. What is the recommended step-by-step workflow for using this platform in a bid round decision?

Licence round evaluation follows a four-phase funnel: jurisdictional screening → comparable regime benchmarking → field-specific DCF calibration → IC memo preparation. ORCA supports all four phases natively.

Phase 1 — Jurisdictional screening (Fiscal Compare + Screener). Load the Fiscal Compare tab — it auto-runs all 185 countries at Deepwater $75/bbl on first visit. This gives you the full ranking of government take by jurisdiction in one view. To narrow to regimes matching your project type, use the Screener: set your take threshold (e.g. <55% for a high-capex deepwater project), filter by mechanic (PSC, Concession), and apply the Deepwater or High IRR preset. The Screener exports filtered results to Excel for team circulation. Rule of thumb: at $75/bbl Deepwater, competitive frontier PSC regimes sit 45–58% take; frontier concessions sit 35–50%; mature OECD concessions sit 48–65%.

Phase 2 — Comparable regime benchmarking (Side-by-Side + Country Profile). Load your shortlisted countries (typically 3–6 finalists) into Side-by-Side for a parallel view of take at $50/$75/$100/$125, Price Swing, IRR (where available), and Breakeven. Side-by-Side exports to PDF — attach directly to the screening memo. For each finalist, open the Country Profile to review: (a) the Reform History timeline — look for reform events in the last 5 years; (b) the Stability Score — any country scoring ≤2 warrants a fiscal risk premium in your IRR hurdle; (c) Evidence badges — A/B tier facts are sourced from primary legislation and operator filings; C/D tier facts are directional estimates. Flag C/D tier data to your IC committee and note that Scenario Builder results for low-evidence countries carry higher model uncertainty.

Phase 3 — Field-specific DCF calibration (Scenario Builder). The platform's reference project ($1.2B capex / 50k bbl/d / $15/bbl opex / 15yr life) is a mid-size deepwater anchor. Your actual block will differ. Use the Scenario Builder to replace the reference project parameters with your block's: (a) capex and opex from your technical team's AFE; (b) peak rate and production profile from your volumetric estimate; (c) contract term matching the offered block duration. Run at $50/$75/$100 to generate your project-specific IRR range. The Scenario Builder is not a full-cycle DCF — it does not model exploration cost, abandonment cost (see A106), or WHT (see A129). Add those in your internal model, using ORCA's regime parameters as fiscal inputs. IC memo language: "Government take at $75/bbl on our project profile: [X]% (ORCA v233 Scenario Builder, [capex]/[opex]/[rate] inputs). Reference project statutory take: [Y]% at $75/bbl Deepwater basis — our project diverges by [+/−Zpp] due to [scale / profile / cost structure] adjustment."

Phase 4 — IC memo finalization. Three items required by most IC committees for a fiscal regime section: (1) Benchmarked take vs. comparable regimes — use the Fiscal Compare XLSX export sorted by take; highlight your target country and 3–5 fiscal peers. (2) Reform risk disclosure — cite the Stability Score and reform history from the Country Profile; note any pending legislative changes (check the Reform History timeline for events in the last 24 months). (3) Standardized take figure with model basis — state the ORCA statutory take, note the reference project profile, and disclose any Scenario Builder adjustment for your field-specific parameters. Add WHT, local content uplift, and exploration cost separately as IC memo line items above the ORCA baseline. Use "How to Cite" at the bottom of this Methodology page for the recommended citation language.

Rule of thumb by bid round stage: Early screening (20+ countries) → Fiscal Compare ranked table; Mid-funnel (5–10 finalists) → Side-by-Side + Screener export; Finalist stage (2–3 countries) → Country Profile deep-dive + Scenario Builder project-specific DCF; IC committee → XLSX export + PDF Side-by-Side + Scenario Builder citation. The platform is designed to carry your analysis from first screening through IC presentation without switching tools. Cross-reference: A37 (IC capital allocation memo workflow — end-to-end process); A51 (Reform Risk Stability Score interpretation — 3-tier screening protocol); A63 (Breakeven + IRR composite project viability screen); A87 (country risk premium / political risk adjustment — IRR hurdle uplift by Stability Score tier); A127 (Breakeven Map vs. Fiscal Compare — when to use each for country screening).

Source: ORCA v233 (Aug 2026). IEA, Upstream Oil and Gas Investment: Risk, Uncertainty, and Decision-Making (2023). SPE, Petroleum Economics and Risk Analysis, 2nd ed. (2021). EY, Global Oil and Gas Tax Guide (2024): bid round fiscal regime descriptions by jurisdiction. Wood Mackenzie, Upstream Fiscal Benchmarking Methodology (2024 subscription, used for reference project calibration). Cross-reference: FAQ A37 (IC capital allocation workflow); FAQ A63 (composite project viability screen); FAQ A87 (country risk premium); FAQ A106 (decommissioning/abandonment obligations — add separately in IC model); FAQ A129 (withholding tax and repatriation risk — add separately in IC model).

A133. I want to build a custom fiscal regime in the Scenario Builder rather than using a country default. How do I calibrate the inputs from a PSA or concession agreement, and how do I interpret the output in an IC context?

When to use Scenario Builder vs. country defaults: ORCA's country-level take figures reflect a production-weighted average of the dominant fiscal mechanic — appropriate for jurisdiction screening (Fiscal Compare, Screener) and initial IC benchmarking. The Scenario Builder is the right tool when: (a) your specific block has materially different terms from the country average (e.g., a new deepwater PSC with a higher cost recovery cap than the country's legacy onshore contracts); (b) you need field-specific IRR and NPV at your own capex/opex/rate assumptions; or (c) the IC committee requires a project-specific take figure with explicit contractual sourcing, not a national average. Rule of thumb: always cross-reference Scenario Builder output against the country profile take — a difference of more than 8pp warrants an explanation in the IC memo.

4-step Scenario Builder calibration workflow:

  1. Identify your fiscal mechanic from the contract: Concession (royalty + CIT, government earns from tax rather than production share), PSC (cost oil + profit oil + CIT on contractor share), TSC/RSC (fee per barrel + CIT — no equity in oil), PRRT (Australia — resource rent tax on post-threshold profit), Buy-back (Iran structure — capital recovery + fixed fee), Revenue Share (gross split without cost recovery). In the Scenario Builder, select the mechanic that matches your contract structure. If the contract contains both a royalty and a profit oil split, it is a PSC (not a Concession), because a Concession earns the state income through tax only — not through a production share.
  2. Read your key fiscal parameters from the PSA or concession agreement:
    • Concession: Royalty rate (often sliding by volume or depth — use expected effective rate); CIT rate (or ring-fence rate where applicable, e.g. UK RFCT 30% + SC 10%); deductibility of capital costs (straight-line depreciation schedule or immediate deduction).
    • PSC: Royalty rate (if any — many PSCs have zero royalty); cost recovery cap (% of gross revenue that may be applied to recover costs in any period — typically 50–80%); profit oil split by R-factor tier or flat (contractor share, not government share); CIT rate on contractor profit oil; FTP (First Tranche Petroleum, if applicable — typically 10–20% of gross production allocated to government before cost recovery).
    • TSC/RSC: Contractor fee per barrel (the primary remuneration element); CIT rate; EPT or excess profit levy (if applicable above a price threshold).
    • PRRT: Use the Australia preset — PRRT rate (40%), uplift rate (LTBR+5% for exploration, LTBR+15% for general), and CIT (30%). PRRT is automatically triggered once the project generates profit in excess of the uplift threshold.
  3. Set your production profile parameters: The Scenario Builder accepts capex ($M), opex ($/bbl), and peak rate (bbl/d). Use your AFE for capex and your P50 volumetric for peak rate. For opex, use lifting cost (not all-in including G&A and corporate overhead — the Scenario Builder opex is field-level). If your project has a cost structure that differs significantly from the ORCA reference (e.g., a giant field at 150k bbl/d vs. the Deepwater reference at 50k bbl/d), the scale difference will affect unit economics. The Scenario Builder does not currently allow you to set a custom production profile shape — it uses the built-in decline curve for the selected profile archetype. For shape-sensitive analysis (R-factor PSCs, PRRT), note that A128 documents the expected direction and magnitude of the shape adjustment.
  4. Interpret and disclose the Scenario Builder output in the IC memo: The Scenario Builder returns: government take (%), contractor NPV ($M), contractor IRR (%), and breakeven price ($/bbl). These are field-specific results reflecting your inputs — not the national average. IC memo disclosure language: "Government take on the [Block X] project at $75/bbl under project-specific terms: [Y]% (ORCA v233 Scenario Builder, $[capex]M capex / [rate]k bbl/d peak / $[opex]/bbl opex / [mechanic] mechanic with [royalty]% royalty, [CR cap]% cost recovery cap, [profit oil split]% contractor profit oil split, [CIT]% CIT). National reference take for [Country]: [Z]% (ORCA country average, [mechanic] dominant, $75/bbl Deepwater basis). Project-specific take diverges from national reference by [Y−Z]pp due to [higher cost recovery cap / higher royalty / project scale / FTP clause / R-factor tiering at this production level]." Do not omit the explanation for any divergence of more than 5pp from the national reference — IC committees will flag unexplained discrepancies between the platform figure and the Scenario Builder output.

Common calibration pitfalls:

  • Confusing royalty base: Most royalties are on gross revenue (production × price). Some are on net revenue after transportation deductions. Use the gross revenue basis unless the contract explicitly states otherwise.
  • Using CIT rate before ring-fence adjustments: UK: use 30% RFCT (not 25% standard CIT) plus the applicable Supplementary Charge (currently 10%, post-EPL); Norway: 78% marginal rate on upstream income (22% ordinary CIT + 56% SPT — do not use 22% alone).
  • PSC profit oil split direction: Enter the contractor share (e.g., 40% contractor / 60% government → enter 40%). The Scenario Builder computes government profit oil as the complement.
  • R-factor PSCs: The Scenario Builder uses the base (R=0) contractor profit oil split. For mid-life R-factor transitions, use A70 (R-factor mechanics) and A128 (decline curve shape) to estimate the production-weighted effective split, then enter that as a flat approximation in the Scenario Builder.
  • FTP vs. no-FTP: If the PSC has a First Tranche Petroleum (FTP = 10–20% of gross production allocated to government before cost recovery), the effective take will be higher than a no-FTP PSC with the same profit oil split. The Scenario Builder FTP field captures this — leave at 0% if not contractually required.

Rule of thumb by mechanic for Scenario Builder vs. country default divergence: Concession: divergence typically under 5pp (royalty and CIT rates are statutory — country default is usually accurate). PSC: divergence can be 5–15pp if block-specific cost recovery cap or FTP differs from country norm. TSC: use Scenario Builder whenever the contract fee differs from ORCA's TSC basis (Iraq TSC country average ≈$2.50/bbl; a specific block may offer $1.80 or $3.20). PRRT: always use country default for Australia unless you are modeling a specific project above threshold with a known development cost base — PRRT output is highly sensitive to project IRR trajectory. Cross-reference: FAQ A70 (R-factor mechanics); FAQ A100 (FTP/first tranche petroleum); FAQ A128 (production decline curve shape and take interaction); FAQ A41 (DCF model specification and IC disclosure requirements).

Source: ORCA v233 (Aug 2026). Johnston, D., International Petroleum Fiscal Systems and Production Sharing Contracts (PennWell, 1994): Chapter 4 (PSC parameter calibration). EY, Global Oil and Gas Tax Guide (2024): CIT/ring-fence rates by jurisdiction. Wood Mackenzie, Upstream Fiscal Benchmarking Methodology (2024 subscription). SPE, Petroleum Economics and Risk Analysis, 2nd ed. (2021): field-level fiscal calibration workflow. Cross-reference: FAQ A37 (IC capital allocation memo workflow); FAQ A41 (IRR DCF model specification); FAQ A70 (R-factor mechanics — profit oil tier calibration); FAQ A100 (FTP first tranche petroleum); FAQ A128 (production decline curve shape interaction with fiscal mechanics).

A134. Our upstream portfolio spans positions in 14 countries across PSC, Concession, and TSC regimes. A single renegotiation wave in West African PSCs would hit 70% of our positions simultaneously. How do I use ORCA to quantify fiscal mechanic concentration risk and present it in a portfolio review?

Why mechanic concentration matters: Government take is not just a country-level variable — it is a mechanic-level variable. PSC profit oil splits, Concession royalty rates, and TSC fee schedules are each vulnerable to distinct policy risks. A portfolio concentrated in PSCs in Sub-Saharan Africa (Nigeria, Angola, Ghana, Tanzania, Mozambique) faces correlated renegotiation risk: a regional PSC reform wave — as occurred in 2011–2014 (Nigeria Petroleum Industry Bill, Angola's PREDD reforms, Mozambique's 2014 taxation changes) — can simultaneously increase effective take across all PSC positions. This systemic fiscal risk is distinct from country-specific political risk and does not diversify within a single mechanic type. Concession regimes face analogous windfall profit tax exposure in high-price environments (e.g., UK EPL 2022, Norway SPT increase 2022). A balanced portfolio identifies where mechanic clustering exceeds tolerable systemic thresholds.

4-step concentration audit workflow using ORCA:

  1. Map your mechanic distribution (IOC Portfolio tab): Load your company on the IOC Portfolio tab. The stats bar shows your mechanic count and weighted average take by country. Read the Mechanic column in the results table and tally the contract-count weight by mechanic type. Rule of thumb thresholds: >60% of contracts in one mechanic type = concentrated; >70% = high concentration risk. The IOC Portfolio tab exports to XLSX (↓ XLSX button) — use this to build the concentration audit table in Excel.
  2. Stress-test your PSC positions (Fiscal Compare + Screener): Run Fiscal Compare at $50/bbl and sort by Swing. PSC regimes in Sub-Saharan Africa show the highest Swing (typically 15–28pp), because R-factor acceleration and high profit oil splits amplify price sensitivity. Filter the Screener to Mechanic = PSC + Region = Africa + Swing > 15pp to identify your highest-concentration/highest-sensitivity cluster. A cluster where 8 of 14 positions share PSC mechanic + Africa region + Swing >15pp is a portfolio-level stress scenario, not just individual country risk.
  3. Identify reform correlation risk (Reform Risk tab): On the Reform Risk tab, check the Regional Reform Tilt panel — it shows whether a region is net-tightening or net-liberalizing. Africa has historically been net-tightening (5–7 tightening events vs. 1–2 liberalizing per 5-year period, 2010–2023). For each country in your PSC cluster, check the Stability Score (0–5 dot scale). A cluster where >3 of 5 PSC countries have Stability Score ≤ 2 means correlated reform risk is not diversified away by geography — it is amplified by regional policy contagion.
  4. Build the IC memo concentration matrix: Report three metrics for the portfolio: (a) Mechanic concentration ratio = % of total contracts (or production-weighted WI%) in the dominant mechanic; (b) Systemic sensitivity = weighted-average Swing for positions in the dominant mechanic cluster (use Screener export for the underlying data); (c) Reform correlation score = % of dominant-mechanic positions in regions with net-tightening reform trend × (1 − average Stability Score). IC memo disclosure template: "Portfolio fiscal mechanic analysis (ORCA v233): [PSC] concentration [X]% of contracts (production-weighted: [Y]%). Systemic price sensitivity (weighted avg Swing, PSC cluster): [Z]pp. Reform correlation risk: [N] of [M] PSC positions in net-tightening regions with Stability Score ≤ 2. Recommended portfolio rebalancing: [target mechanic allocation] to reduce systemic sensitivity below [threshold]pp."

What ORCA does and does not capture for concentration analysis: ORCA captures statutory fiscal mechanic (Concession, PSC, TSC, PRRT, RSC, Buy-back, Revenue Share, Gross Split) at the country level using the dominant mechanic by contract count. It does not model: (a) specific block-level contractual terms that may diverge from country norms (use Scenario Builder per block); (b) hedging instruments or fiscal stabilization clauses that may dampen reform exposure (see FAQ A103); (c) production-weighted WI shares (the IOC Portfolio table shows contract counts, not WI% — weight by your actual WI% in the XLSX output for a production-adjusted view). The concentration analysis using ORCA is a first-order screen. Second-order analysis (which stabilization clauses actually hedge the PSC positions; what prior reform events affected which specific blocks) requires data room materials and contract-by-contract review.

Rule of thumb by mechanic type for systemic risk: PSC (especially Sub-Saharan Africa and Southeast Asia): highest reform risk, highest Swing — systemic threshold >50% of contracts warrants a portfolio-level mitigation plan (Scenario Builder stress-test at tightened terms; identify Stability Score ≥4 PSC alternatives). Concession (OECD): low reform risk in normal environments, but windfall profit tax exposure in high-price scenarios — apply UK EPL or Norway SPT analogy if Swing >10pp and price >$90/bbl. TSC (Iraq, Kuwait): structurally low take (fee per barrel) and low Swing — diversifying concentration with TSC positions reduces both average take and systemic sensitivity. PRRT (Australia): reform stable since 2012 uplift amendment; concentration risk low for portfolios with Woodside/Santos-type exposure. Rule: the systemic risk score (concentration ratio × average Swing) should not exceed 15 for any mechanic cluster in a healthy portfolio (e.g., 60% PSC × 25pp avg Swing = 15 — borderline; 70% × 22pp = 15.4 — exceeds threshold).

Source: ORCA v233 (Aug 2026). IMF Fiscal Affairs Department (2012), “Fiscal Regimes for Extractive Industries: Design and Implementation.” IEA, “World Energy Investment” (2023): IOC portfolio allocation and regime-type diversification. Wood Mackenzie (2022), “West African Upstream Fiscal Reform Risk: PSC Renegotiation Wave Assessment.” Nigeria Petroleum Industry Act 2021 (fiscal reform context). Angola Presidential Decree 55/18 (2018 PSC fiscal adjustment). Tanzania Natural Resources (Permanent Sovereignty) Act 2017. Mozambique Law 27/2014 (petroleum taxation reform). ORCA Reform History database: regional tightening/liberalizing event counts 2010–2023.
